clinicalPearls: SLAC is the most common pattern of degenerative wrist arthritis and usually arises from untreated scapholunate dissociation.
Degeneration follows a predictable sequence: the radial styloid-scaphoid articulation first, then the whole radioscaphoid joint, then the capitolunate and midcarpal joint.
The radiolunate joint is characteristically spared, which underpins motion-preserving salvage procedures.
Scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC) follows an analogous but distinct degenerative pattern originating from scaphoid nonunion.
Stage guides surgery: radial styloidectomy with scapholunate treatment early, proximal row carpectomy or scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion later, and total wrist fusion for pancarpal disease.
Proximal row carpectomy depends on preserved cartilage on the capitate head and in the lunate fossa.
Wrist denervation via anterior and posterior interosseous neurectomy can relieve pain while preserving motion in selected patients.
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic scapholunate dissociation allows the scaphoid to assume a fixed flexed and rotated position, shifting radiocarpal contact to a small area at the radial styloid. Abnormal, concentrated loading erodes articular cartilage first at the radioscaphoid articulation and then across the midcarpal joint as the capitate migrates proximally into the gap between scaphoid and lunate. Because the lunate remains congruent within the lunate fossa, the radiolunate joint is preserved, which allows salvage operations that offload the diseased articulations while retaining some wrist motion.
additionalDifferentials: Post-traumatic radiocarpal arthritis from an intra-articular distal radius fracture
additionalInvestigations: PA and lateral radiographs to stage the degenerative pattern
CT for detailed articular assessment and surgical planning
MRI to evaluate cartilage and the capitate head before proximal row carpectomy
Diagnostic wrist arthroscopy to grade chondral surfaces
Inflammatory and crystal screen if an inflammatory arthropathy is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive pain and deformity suggesting advanced collapse
Features of inflammatory or crystal arthropathy requiring systemic work-up
Capitate head chondral loss that would contraindicate proximal row carpectomy
reference.prognosis: SLAC is progressive and non-reversible, but stage-appropriate salvage surgery reliably relieves pain, albeit at the cost of some grip strength and wrist motion.
pitfalls: Choosing proximal row carpectomy when the capitate head cartilage is already compromised.
Failing to distinguish SLAC from SNAC, which changes the pattern of joint involvement.
Mistaking crystal or inflammatory arthropathy for degenerative SLAC.
Underestimating radial styloid involvement in early disease.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
